quarterly_data.signal: Q4 2025 results: revenue 'came in about as expected at $4.4 billion, a decrease of 7% sequentially and an increase of 10% from the same quarter a year ago'; Analog revenue grew 14% year over year, Embedded processing grew 8%, and the Other segment declined. Gross profit $2.5 billion or 56% of revenue (down 150 basis points sequentially); operating expenses $967 million (up 3% YoY); operating profit $1.5 billion or 33% of revenue (up 7% YoY); net income $1.2 billion or $1.27 per share, including a 6¢ reduction not in the original guidance for a non-cash goodwill impairment in the Other segment and other tax-related items. Q4 cash flow from operations $2.3 billion; capital expenditures $925 million. CEO: 'The overall semiconductor market recovery is continuing, and we are well-positioned with inventory and capacity to meet immediate customer demand.'
quarterly_data.figure: Revenue $4.4 billion (-7% sequentially, +10% YoY); Analog +14%; gross margin 56%; operating margin 33%; EPS $1.27

quarterly_data.signal: TI reorganized its end markets to add DATA CENTER — 'sectors related to data center compute, data center networking, and rack power and thermal management' — so its end markets are now industrial, automotive, data center, personal electronics and communications equipment. In Q4 2025 data center 'grew around 70% year on year and mid-single digits sequentially'; full-year 2025 data center revenue was $1.5 billion, up 64% year on year and 9% of revenue. CEO: data center has been 'growing for now seven quarters in a row', 'we left the year at about $450 million a quarter revenue footprint', and he expects it to keep growing in Q1 2026; it is 'now a bigger part of our business. It starts to move the numbers for us' and helped the above-seasonal Q1 guide. He expects the growth to continue 'as CapEx continues to be invested in data centers'.
quarterly_data.figure: Data center ~70% YoY in Q4 2025; 2025 data center revenue $1.5 billion (+64%, 9% of revenue); exit rate about $450 million a quarter

quarterly_data.signal: Data-center positioning (CEO): the data-center business is analog-based across power and signal chain — 'maybe a little bit more power, but both power and signal chain are very strong in data center'. Beyond the very large VRM / VCORE voltage-regulator socket, 'if you look at the rack and you open it up, there are thousands of different parts, and many of them are analog embedded parts', and TI plays across the board. TI has invested in technology for the higher-power rails (VCore, where much of the current going into an accelerator or CPU comes from), which TI is building in Sherman, Texas, where its BCD process 'is serving us very well': 'That product is sampling, and we expect our opportunity in data center to further expand in the coming years.' TI plans to play across the different data-center sockets as long as CapEx continues into this market.
quarterly_data.figure: VCore high-power-rail product sampling (BCD process, Sherman, Texas); thousands of different parts per rack

quarterly_data.signal: Estimated 2025 revenue by end market: Industrial $5.8 billion (up 12%, 33% of revenue); Automotive $5.8 billion (up 6%, 33%); Data center $1.5 billion (up 64%, 9%); Personal electronics $3.7 billion (up 7%, 21%); Communications equipment about $500 million (up about 20%, 3%). Industrial, automotive and data center combined were about 75% of revenue in 2025, up from about 43% in 2013. Q4 2025 by end market: industrial up high teens YoY (18%) and down mid-single digits sequentially; automotive up upper single digits YoY and down low single digits sequentially; personal electronics down upper teens YoY and mid-teens sequentially (TV/home theater weakest, mobile phones best, China subsidies expiring); communications equipment down low single digits YoY and mid-teens sequentially. China revenue was down about 7% sequentially and up about 16% YoY in Q4. Industrial's highest 2025 quarter (Q3) was still about 25% below its 2022 peak; automotive is back to roughly its Q3 2023 peak level on content-per-vehicle secular growth, and Q1 is seasonally down for autos in China (Chinese New Year).
quarterly_data.figure: 2025: Industrial $5.8 billion (+12%), Automotive $5.8 billion (+6%), Personal electronics $3.7 billion (+7%), Communications equipment about $500 million; industrial + automotive + data center about 75% of revenue

quarterly_data.signal: Q1 2026 guidance: revenue $4.32 billion to $4.68 billion and EPS $1.22 to $1.48; 2026 effective tax rate about 13 to 14%; OPEX up low single digits. Management called the guide 'maybe a little bit above seasonal' versus the usual 'Low single-digit decline to flattish' first quarter, driven by orders: 'we did see orders improving throughout the quarter. And what guides our guidance is the stronger booking'. Revenue linearity and backlog built month to month through Q4, turns (ship-right-away) business ran at higher levels, and customers are placing orders 'a little bit more forward'. The above-seasonal guide is 'not pricing related'; data center's larger share also changes the guide versus prior years. Factory loadings will be adjusted to demand, with nothing significant changing versus Q4.
quarterly_data.figure: Q1 2026 revenue $4.32 billion to $4.68 billion; EPS $1.22 to $1.48

quarterly_data.signal: Pricing and supply posture: asked whether TI is raising prices in Q1 2026 (analysts cited peers discussing early-2026 increases), the CEO said 'the answer is no. It's not pricing related' — the like-for-like price effect in 2025 finished low single digits down as expected ('think about two or 3% down'), and that is also TI's assumption for 2026, though TI would respond if pricing conditions change; Q1 pricing usually goes down a little because of yearly negotiations, with 'Definitely no step function planned in Q1'. Lead times are unchanged, 'on average, below thirteen weeks', 'probably the lowest in the industry'. Inventory ended Q4 at $4.8 billion (down $25 million QoQ; 222 days), which management calls an asset for real-time demand, and TI is 'well-positioned with capacity'. The CEO noted 'we all know about the memory shortages', and management said customers that finally complete their bill of materials have come in at the last minute wanting product shipped right away.
quarterly_data.figure: 2025 price effect low single digits down (two or 3%), same assumption for 2026; lead times below thirteen weeks; inventory $4.8 billion (222 days)

quarterly_data.signal: Manufacturing (CEO): the Sherman fab 'ramped ahead of schedule, high yield', and with its new equipment the factory is 'more capable than we originally hoped', so a high level of throughput is planned; Sherman one's clean room already has some production lines running, and TI has additional shell space ('Shell instrument two' as transcribed) it can build into if demand is very strong. The 'Lehigh' fab (as transcribed) is on schedule, insourcing wafers from foundries — mainly embedded processing, a tailwind that continues in 2026: TI completed its 65-nanometer transition in 2025, yielding at the same level as in the foundries, and is now moving its 45-nanometer technology, mainly for its automotive radar business. CFO: TI is 'nearing the end of a six-year elevated CapEx cycle' that positions it to deliver 'dependable low-cost 300-millimeter capacity at scale'.
quarterly_data.figure: 65-nanometer foundry insourcing completed in 2025; 45-nanometer in progress; Sherman ramped ahead of schedule

quarterly_data.signal: Capital plan (CFO): 2026 CapEx still expected 'between $2 and $3 billion'; new 2026 depreciation guide of $2.2 to $2.4 billion, with 'upward pressure' again in 2027 but at a slower rate of increase. CHIPS Act direct funding unchanged at up to $1.6 billion as milestones are reached; the investment tax credit 'is now 35% as of 01/01/2026', applying to 2026 equipment, building and clean-room spend. In 2025 TI received a $670 million cash benefit related to CHIPS Act incentives. Beyond 2026, gross CapEx runs about 1.2 times long-term revenue growth (10% growth gives 12% capital intensity) before ITC, essentially one to one net; the CEO characterized maintenance CapEx as mid-single-digit of revenue. 2025 cash flow from operations was $7.2 billion and free cash flow $2.9 billion or 17% of revenue, up 96% from 2024. Q4 dividends $1.3 billion and buybacks $403 million; the dividend was raised 4% to $1.42 per share (twenty-second consecutive year of increases); $6.5 billion returned in the past twelve months. A capital management call was scheduled for February 24.
quarterly_data.figure: 2026 CapEx between $2 and $3 billion; 2026 depreciation $2.2 to $2.4 billion; ITC 35%; 2025 free cash flow $2.9 billion (+96%)
